question.note: Phrased as what the paper argues rather than as a question, but its subject is the spillover of the 'convicted criminal' ad onto perceptions of people with records (Q1).
States the counter-narrative's mitigating effect; its subject is Q2. Could instead be read as a misplaced half of C1.

flags.text: 'Exposure to a stigmatizing label of Trump' attributes the effect to the label; the stimulus was the mugshot with the label, and the paper says the two cannot be disentangled (p.17). The quotes say 'advertisement with the ... label'.

central_claim.note: Gives the harm to perceptions and the counter-narrative's mitigation; omits that the ad improved feelings of representation, although the first quote says so.

evidence.note: Names the three arms, without the counts.
Prolific and the July 12-13, 2025 dates (the rest of E1; 2,500 recruited is the paper's pre-exclusion figure), plus the manipulation check on emotional reactions (E7).

flags.text: 'Exposure to a stigmatizing label of convicted criminal' attributes the effect to the label; the stimulus was the mugshot with the label, and the paper says the two cannot be disentangled (p.17). The quote says 'advertisement with the ... label'.

'The negative effects of stigmatizing language' attributes the ad's effect to the language; the paper's quote speaks of 'the negative effects of the advertisement', and image and label cannot be separated (p.17).

key_findings.note: Keeps the offset relation to the ad's effect, so no F-x2 flag.

flags.text: Says the counter-narrative increased perceived public-service motives of officials. The paper finds it reduced them relative to the ad alone (H1F, beta = -0.098, p.11, not robust to Bonferroni). The quote is a hypothesis. The value-of-representation half is accurate (H1C, p.11).
